title: Mara, Part 1
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart suggests that Mara, often seen as an obstacle on the Buddhist path, can actually be viewed as a shadowy representation of humanity's own attachments and ego. By recognizing this dualistic relationship, practitioners can transform their negative tendencies into positive ones, much like gardeners turning garbage into compost. This understanding encourages us to look beyond our usual tendency to see things as separate from ourselves, instead embracing the interconnectedness and interdependence of all phenomena.

sentences.text: I would like to thank Tim for inviting me to give a talk tonight.
I would also like to thank Kate for her excellent talk on kleshas last month.
She described kleshas as obstacles or hindrances on the Buddhist path and obstacles to our practice.
Kleshas are interesting—our avoidance, the tendency to flee the difficult, to flee reality by distracting ourselves, by seeking entertainment.
Instead of opening to emptiness, the empty nature of all things, we seek security and permanence.
One could say that it is a human instinct to try to find our own permanence in phenomena.
So I thought I would continue a bit on that klesha path.
Tonight I would like to talk about the personification of kleshas, the mother of all kleshas, Mara.
I will be offering views that may differ from the way we usually talk about Mara, the evil one.
And as always, I would like you to look at my talk as a tentative teaching.
I am quite sure I will change my mind about quite a few things, so please look at it as something tentative, open to discussion.
So here is a very old story about Mara.
This is an account of his visit to Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha-to-be, just before his enlightenment.
Gautama was sitting under the Bodhi tree, with a firm resolve to become a Buddha.
And when Mara saw Gautama and saw his strong intention to become a Buddha, he summoned his forces, ten legions, to attack him.
Mara's forces extended leagues behind him and to the side.
They were armed with deadly weapons and had assumed terrifying forms.
But Gautama defeated them through the paramitas: generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, honesty, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity.
Still, Mara did not give up.
Mara claimed Gautama's seat under the Bodhi tree as his own because, he said, he had achieved perfect generosity and kindness.
And his followers loudly affirmed his claim.
Mara then asked Gautama to prove his right to the seat.
And seeing that Gautama was alone, he asked who would affirm his claim.
So Gautama touched the ground and the earth roared in response: "I stand his witness."
Thus Mara was defeated.
And weeping over his defeat, he left.
Throughout the Buddha's life, Mara continues to show up, to tempt, to mislead, or terrify the Buddha.

I will just mention a few of his methods: by telling the Buddha he should not have given up the austerities; by taking on beautiful or ugly forms to tempt or disturb the Buddha; by offering him riches or power; by saying that the Buddha remained bound in samsara; by reprimanding the Buddha for taking a nap—a Buddha should always meditate; by saying that the human lifespan is so long that no one needs to worry about the spiritual life.
In all cases, the Buddha sees and understands what is happening—that this is an encounter with Mara—and he directly responds to Mara every time, addressing him by name.
Oh, this is Mara, the evil one.
The Buddha then addresses the temptation, lie, or illusion.
And then all the sutras end the same way: then Mara, the evil one, realizing, "Oh, the blessed one knows me.
The fortunate one knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
So I would like to read you one of those brief sutras.
*It's called The Splinter.
Thus have I heard.
On one occasion the blessed one was dwelling at Rajagaha at Deer Park.
Now, on that occasion, the blessed one's foot had been cut by a stone splinter.
Severe pains assailed the blessed one.
Bodily feelings that were painful, racking, sharp, piercing, harrowing, disagreeable.
But the blessed one endured them.
Mindful and clearly comprehending without becoming distressed.*
Then the blessed one had his outer robe folded in four, and he lay down on his right side in the lying posture, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Then Mara, the evil one, approached the blessed one and addressed him in verse: "Do you lie down in a daze or drunk on poetry?
Don't you have sufficient goals to meet?
Alone in a secluded lodging, why do you sleep with a drowsy face?"
The blessed one replied, "I do not lie in a daze or drunk on poetry.
Having reached the goal, I am rid of sorrow.
Alone in a secluded lodging, I lie down, full of compassion for all beings, even those with a dart stuck in their breast, piercing their heart moment by moment.
Even these here, stricken, go to sleep.
So why should I not get to sleep when my dart has been drawn out?
I do not lie awake in dread, nor am I afraid to sleep.
The nights and days do not afflict me.
I see for myself no decline in the world.
Therefore I can sleep in peace, full of compassion for all beings."
Then the evil one, realizing, "Oh, the blessed one knows me.
The fortunate one knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right here.
So this is the evil one, Mara.
We know and don't love Mara, the master illusionist who needs to control or own everything.
It is clear that the Buddha, by seeing and understanding Mara, does not get caught.
By clearly seeing the snare for what it is, he is not confused and does not fall into the trap.
So this now is the difficult part: how do we recognize Mara?
Because he's not necessarily a drooling devil with horns and a pitchfork.
Mara can look very good and successful.
Mara knows all about spiritual journeys, and he knows the lingo.
It often appears that he's trying to help the Buddha or encourage him to make greater effort: "Don't sleep when the sun is up."
That is sloth.
"Show equanimity by not giving in to your pain."
Mara has great confidence and is very certain of himself.
True, once caught, he says, "the blessed one knows me," in a pitiful voice and then slinks away.
But up to that point, he sure seems to use all the right words and phrases.
He does seem to have many attributes of the Buddha.
So in this world, on this path full of pitfalls, how can I keep them apart?
Is it the Buddha in self-compassion needing to sleep?
Or is it Mara wanting to be lazy?
We need to be very careful.
I believe the test is going to be the three marks of Buddhism: impermanence, dissatisfaction or suffering, and non-self.
If we pay attention, we see that Mara is pushing us towards confirming the self.
He seeks material or spiritual possessions.
He makes things more concrete and solid.
He likes his stuff.
But still, something remains off in this opposing picture of Buddha and Mara—the classic battle between good and evil fought on all levels of existence.
So now I'm coming to the point that hopefully will encourage a conversation later on.
So let us go back to the enlightenment story.
What if?
What if Mara never appeared to challenge Gautama?
I say Mara did not show up just before the Buddha reached enlightenment.
I believe that Mara sat with the Buddha under the Bodhi tree the whole time.
I believe that they hungered together, that they meditated together.
Gotama and Mara were the two sides of the coin.
Mara clings to possessions, attachment, gain, fortune.
In the early Pali suttas, Mara appears as the voice of doubt and uncertainty, which the Buddha hears, understands, and overcomes.
Can we see Mara as Buddha's shadow, counter-image, his own conflict with humanity?
In later sutras, Mara became theological doctrine.
At the same time, the Buddha was elevated higher and higher until he was not human anymore but enlightenment itself.
Is this a dualistic way of seeing Buddha and Mara?
So I would like to close this talk with a somewhat long quote by Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh.
He said it beautifully: "You may compare Buddha with the flowers, very fresh, very beautiful.
And you may compare Mara with the garbage.
It doesn't smell good.
There are a lot of flies.
It's not pleasant to touch, to hold in your hand, to smell the garbage.
Yet all flowers become garbage."
That is the meaning of impermanence.
All flowers have to become garbage.
If you practice Buddhist meditation, you find out about very interesting things, like about the garbage.
Although garbage stinks, although garbage is not pleasant to hold in your hand, if you know how to take care of the garbage, you will transform it back into flowers.
You know gardeners don't throw away garbage.
They preserve the garbage and take care of the garbage.
And in just a few months, the garbage becomes compost.
They can use that compost to grow lettuce, tomatoes, and flowers.
We have to say that organic gardeners are capable of seeing flowers in garbage, seeing cucumbers in garbage.
That is what the Buddha described as the non-dualistic way of looking at things.
